summary: On the border of Samaria and Galilee, Jesus cleanses ten lepers with a word; only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank Him.
key_insight: The nine were doing exactly what Jesus told them: going to show themselves to the priests. The Samaritan turned back instead, and Jesus calls his return to fall at His feet a return “to give glory to God.” Thanking Jesus is glorifying God.
story: On the way to Jerusalem, Jesus passed along between Samaria and Galilee. As He entered a certain village, ten men who were lepers met Him. They stood afar off and lifted up their voices: “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!”
When Jesus saw them, He said to them, “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” They went, and as they went, they were cleansed.
One of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back. With a loud voice he glorified God, and he fell down on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving Him thanks. And he was a Samaritan.
Jesus said, “Were there not ten cleansed? But where are the nine? Were there not any found who returned to give glory to God except this foreigner?”
Then He said to him, “Arise, go your way. Your faith has made you well.”

scene.label: From Ephraim to the border
scene.text: John last placed Jesus at Ephraim, near the wilderness north of Jerusalem (John 11:54). Luke now has Him passing “through the midst of Samaria and Galilee,” most likely along the border between them, toward the Jordan valley and the pilgrim road south to Jericho. Edersheim suggests He went to meet followers from Galilee for the Passover journey, among them the “many other women who came up with Him to Jerusalem” (Mark 15:41); the Gospels do not say.

scene.label: A company of outcasts
scene.text: The Law required lepers to live apart (Leviticus 13:46), so the ten called out from a distance. Jews and Samaritans normally kept apart too, but disease had pushed this Samaritan and his companions, apparently Jews, into one company of outcasts.

scene.label: To the priests
scene.text: A healed leper had to be examined by a priest before he could go home and return to worship (Leviticus 14:2–3). Jesus sent the ten off while they were still diseased, so setting out was itself an act of trust in His word.

scene.label: “This foreigner”
scene.text: Jesus’ word for the Samaritan appears nowhere else in the New Testament. It is the word carved on the stone notices along the barrier in the temple courts, warning that any foreigner who went further would be put to death. The man barred from the inner courts is the one who came back to give glory to God.

scene.label: Naaman returned
scene.text: Jesus had reminded Nazareth that in Elisha’s day the only leper cleansed was “Naaman the Syrian” (Luke 4:27). He too was a foreigner, and after washing in the Jordan, “he returned to the man of God” (2 Kings 5:15) and confessed the God of Israel.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke tells this story, and it carries two of his favorite threads: thanks and praise to God, and the outsider who responds while insiders do not, as with the good Samaritan (10:33). Luke marks it with a fresh reminder that Jesus was going to Jerusalem (17:11), and McGarvey and Edersheim both take it as the opening of the last journey, after the stay at Ephraim (John 11:54).

seeing.reveals: Jesus’ word alone cleanses ten men at a distance. And He notices who comes back: He counts the ten, asks after the nine, and sends the one away with a personal word about his faith.
seeing.living: Nine received the gift and kept walking toward the life it gave back to them. Gratitude turns back to the Giver first, and says it out loud, as the Samaritan did. When Jesus answers a prayer, do not hurry on to the next thing before you have thanked Him.
seeing.ponder: What has Jesus done for you that you have never come back to thank Him for?

preaching.big_idea: Many receive Jesus’ gifts; few return to His feet with thanks.
preaching.watch_for: Watch the verb “returned” (vv. 15, 18) and the Samaritan’s place “at His feet” (v. 16). Jesus’ last word, “Your faith has made you well,” uses a verb that also means saved, and many see in it more than the healing all ten received.
